notes.front: What is a leak inspection?
notes.back: An examination of an appliance to find the location of refrigerant leaks.
notes.explanation: Methods named include ultrasonic tests, gas-imaging cameras, bubble tests and properly maintained leak detection devices, among others.
notes.example: Like tracing a damp patch back to the pipe joint that drips, rather than only noticing the water bill has gone up.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions, “Leak inspection”
notes.evidence: Leak inspection means the examination of an appliance to determine the location of refrigerant leaks. Potential methods include, but are not limited to, ultrasonic tests, gas-imaging cameras, bubble tests as appropriate, or the use of a leak detection device operated and maintained according to manufacturer guidelines.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: For which low-pressure appliances does the Type III outline ask for a maximum leak test pressure?
notes.back: Low-pressure centrifugal chillers.
notes.explanation: The outline names the item under leak detection for low-pressure systems; the page itself does not give the pressure figure.
notes.example: Like the large chiller in the plant room of an office tower.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Leak Detection”
notes.evidence: Maximum leak test pressure for low-pressure centrifugal chillers

notes.front: What is a chronically leaking appliance?
notes.back: One containing 50 pounds or more of refrigerant that leaks 125 percent or more of its full charge in a calendar year.
notes.explanation: Its owner or operator must submit a report on it to the Agency.
notes.example: Like a system holding 200 pounds that needs more than 250 pounds put back in over a single calendar year.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(j), Chronically leaking appliances
notes.evidence: Owners or operators of appliances containing 50 pounds or more of refrigerant that leak 125 percent or more of the full charge in a calendar year must submit a report to EPA
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: The purge unit's purpose is a Type III test topic. Which purging-related sign of leakage into a low-pressure system does the outline give?
notes.back: Excessive purging.
notes.explanation: The outline gives excessive purging as an example (“e.g.”), so it need not be the only sign.
notes.example: Like a sump pump that switches on far more often than usual, hinting that water is getting in somewhere.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Leak Detection”
notes.evidence: Signs of leakage into a low-pressure system (e.g., excessive purging)

notes.front: Through which valve does the Type III outline say centrifugals should be charged?
notes.back: The evaporator charging valve.
notes.explanation: It is listed under recharging techniques, next to introducing vapour before liquid.
notes.example: Like filling a car's coolant through its own filler cap rather than through any opening that happens to fit.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recharging Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to introduce vapor before liquid to prevent freezing of water in the tubes - Need to charge centrifugals through evaporator charging valve

notes.front: In the Type III outline's order of leak test pressurisation methods for low-pressure systems, what comes first?
notes.back: The hot water method, or a built-in system heating/pressurisation device such as Prevac.
notes.explanation: These methods head the order, with nitrogen listed after them.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Leak Detection”
notes.evidence: Order of preference of leak test pressurization methods for low-pressure systems - Hot water method or built-in system heating/pressurization device such Prevac - Nitrogen

notes.front: Which leak test pressurisation method does the Type III outline list after hot water or a built-in heating device?
notes.back: Nitrogen.
notes.explanation: It is second in the outline's order of preference for low-pressure systems.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Leak Detection”
notes.evidence: Order of preference of leak test pressurization methods for low-pressure systems - Hot water method or built-in system heating/pressurization device such Prevac - Nitrogen

notes.front: A technician must raise the pressure in a low-pressure centrifugal chiller to leak test it, and it has a built-in heating/pressurisation device. Which method does the Type III outline prefer?
notes.back: C) The built-in heating/pressurisation device.
notes.choices:
A) Pure refrigerant
B) Nitrogen
C) The built-in heating/pressurisation device
notes.choicesExplained: B: nitrogen comes after hot water or a built-in device in the order. A: the Type III order does not list pure refrigerant.
notes.explanation: Hot water or a built-in device such as Prevac comes first in the outline's order.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Leak Detection”
notes.evidence: Order of preference of leak test pressurization methods for low-pressure systems - Hot water method or built-in system heating/pressurization device such Prevac - Nitrogen

notes.front: The purge unit on a low-pressure chiller has been running far more than usual. What does the Type III outline say this may signal?
notes.back: C) Leakage into the system.
notes.choices:
A) Normal operation
B) An overcharge of refrigerant
C) Leakage into the system
notes.choicesExplained: B: the outline links excessive purging to leakage, not to overcharge. A: the outline treats excessive purging as a sign of leakage.
notes.explanation: Excessive purging is the outline's example of a sign of leakage into a low-pressure system.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Leak Detection”
notes.evidence: Signs of leakage into a low-pressure system (e.g., excessive purging)

notes.front: How often must a commercial refrigeration or IPR appliance with a full charge of 500 pounds or more that exceeded its trigger rate have a leak inspection?
notes.back: Once every three months, until it has not leaked above the rate for four quarters in a row.
notes.explanation: The owner or operator shows the four clean quarters through the leak rate calculations.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(1)(i), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: leak inspections must be conducted once every three months until the owner or operator can demonstrate through the leak rate calculations required under paragraph (b) of this section that the appliance has not leaked in excess of the applicable leak rate for four quarters in a row.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How often must a commercial refrigeration or IPR appliance of 50 to under 500 pounds that exceeded its trigger rate have a leak inspection?
notes.back: Once per calendar year, until it has not leaked above the rate for one year.
notes.explanation: Below 500 pounds, the same two sectors drop from quarterly to annual inspections.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(1)(ii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: with a full charge of 50 or more pounds but less than 500 pounds, leak inspections must be conducted once per calendar year until the owner or operator can demonstrate through the leak rate calculations required under paragraph (b) of this section that the appliance has not leaked in excess of the applicable leak rate for one year.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How often must a comfort cooling appliance that exceeded its trigger rate have a leak inspection?
notes.back: Once per calendar year, whatever its size.
notes.explanation: The quarterly schedule covers only commercial refrigeration and IPR appliances of 500 pounds or more; comfort cooling falls under the annual rule.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(1)(iii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: For comfort cooling appliances and other appliances not covered by paragraphs (g)(1)(i) and (ii) of this section, leak inspections must be conducted once per calendar year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A supermarket rack with an 800-pound full charge has exceeded its trigger rate. How often must it now have a leak inspection?
notes.back: Once every three months.
notes.explanation: It is commercial refrigeration with a full charge of 500 pounds or more.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(1)(i), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: For commercial refrigeration and industrial process refrigeration appliances with a full charge of 500 or more pounds, leak inspections must be conducted once every three months
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A 300-pound industrial process refrigeration unit has exceeded its trigger rate. How often must it have a leak inspection?
notes.back: Once per calendar year.
notes.explanation: It is IPR, but under 500 pounds, so the annual schedule applies.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(1)(ii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: For commercial refrigeration and industrial process refrigeration appliances with a full charge of 50 or more pounds but less than 500 pounds, leak inspections must be conducted once per calendar year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A 1,000-pound comfort cooling chiller in an office tower has exceeded its trigger rate. How often must it have a leak inspection?
notes.back: B) Once per calendar year.
notes.choices:
A) Once every three months, because it is over 500 pounds
B) Once per calendar year
C) Never, because comfort cooling is exempt
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 500-pound quarterly rule covers only commercial refrigeration and IPR. C: comfort cooling appliances that exceed the rate must be inspected.
notes.explanation: Size alone does not bring a comfort cooling appliance into the quarterly schedule.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(1)(iii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: For comfort cooling appliances and other appliances not covered by paragraphs (g)(1)(i) and (ii) of this section, leak inspections must be conducted once per calendar year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Who must conduct a required leak inspection, and who chooses the method?
notes.back: A certified technician, using the method or methods the technician judges appropriate for that appliance.
notes.explanation: The rule sets who inspects but leaves the choice of method to the technician.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(2), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Leak inspections must be conducted by a certified technician using method(s) determined by the technician to be appropriate for that appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which components of an appliance must a leak inspection cover?
notes.back: All visible and accessible components, with some exceptions.
notes.explanation: The exceptions cover inaccessible parts, parts needing work more than two metres up, and parts unsafe to inspect.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(3), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: All visible and accessible components of an appliance must be inspected, with the following exceptions: (i) Where components are insulated, under ice that forms on the outside of equipment, underground, behind walls, or are otherwise inaccessible; (ii) Where personnel must be elevated more than two meters above a support surface; or (iii) Where components are unsafe to inspect
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which kinds of hidden components are excepted from a leak inspection?
notes.back: Components that are insulated, under ice on the equipment, underground, behind walls, or otherwise inaccessible.
notes.explanation: These are all cases where the component cannot be reached for inspection.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(3)(i), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Where components are insulated, under ice that forms on the outside of equipment, underground, behind walls, or are otherwise inaccessible;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What height exception applies to leak inspections?
notes.back: Components are excepted where personnel must be elevated more than two metres above a support surface.
notes.explanation: The rule measures the height from a support surface, not from the ground.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(3)(ii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Where personnel must be elevated more than two meters above a support surface;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Who decides whether a component is too unsafe to include in a leak inspection?
notes.back: Site personnel.
notes.explanation: The exception covers components unsafe to inspect as determined by site personnel.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(3)(iii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Where components are unsafe to inspect, as determined by site personnel.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A valve sits where a technician would have to be raised three metres above the plant-room floor. Must it be included in the leak inspection?
notes.back: No: it falls under the exception for more than two metres above a support surface.
notes.explanation: Three metres is over the two-metre limit, so this component is excepted.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(3)(ii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Where personnel must be elevated more than two meters above a support surface;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Can a pressure check or a sight glass check on its own count as a leak inspection?
notes.back: No: methods that show whether an appliance leaks, but not where, must be used with methods that locate leaks.
notes.explanation: A leak inspection is about location, so methods that only detect a leak are not enough on their own.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions, “Leak inspection”
notes.evidence: Methods that determine whether the appliance is leaking refrigerant but not the location of a leak, such as standing pressure/vacuum decay tests, sight glass checks, viewing receiver levels, pressure checks, and charging charts, must be used in conjunction with methods that can determine the location of a leak.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: After a leak inspection on an appliance with 50 or more pounds of ozone-depleting refrigerant, what are two things the technician's documentation must include?
notes.back: For example, the date of inspection and a list of the location of each leak found (among others).
notes.explanation: The documentation also gives the methods used and a certification that all visible and accessible parts were inspected.
notes.source: EPA, Refrigerant Management Program: Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Questions on Servicing Appliances with 50 or More Pounds of Ozone-Depleting Refrigerant”
notes.evidence: you must provide the customer with documentation that includes the date of inspection; the method(s) used to conduct the leak inspection; a list of the location(s) of each leak that was identified; and a certification that all visible and accessible parts of the appliance were inspected.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: When are quarterly or annual leak inspections not required?
notes.back: On appliances, or parts of them, continuously monitored by an automatic leak detection system that is audited or calibrated annually.
notes.explanation: The exemption holds only while the system is audited or calibrated every year.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(4), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Quarterly or annual leak inspections are not required on appliances, or portions of appliances, continuously monitored by an automatic leak detection system that is audited or calibrated annually.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: For an automatic leak detection system that senses refrigerant in air, what must it detect, and when must it alert the owner?
notes.back: It must detect 10 parts per million, and alert at 100 parts per million.
notes.explanation: Both figures refer to vapour of the specific refrigerant used in the appliance.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(4)(i), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Accurately detect a concentration level of 10 parts per million of vapor of the specific refrigerant or refrigerants used in the refrigeration appliance(s); and (D) Alert the owner or operator when a refrigerant concentration of 100 parts per million of vapor
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Where may an automatic leak detection system that senses refrigerant in air be used?
notes.back: Only to monitor components inside an enclosed building or structure.
notes.explanation: Its sensors must sit near the compressor, evaporator, condenser and other high-risk areas.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(4)(i), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: Only be used to monitor components located inside an enclosed building or structure; (B) Have sensors or intakes placed so that they will continuously monitor the refrigerant concentrations in air in proximity to the compressor, evaporator, condenser, and other areas with a high potential for a refrigerant leak;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A system that monitors appliance conditions, not refrigerant in air, watches a 300-pound appliance. At what loss must it alert the owner?
notes.back: 30 pounds.
notes.explanation: The alert is at 50 pounds or 10 percent of full charge, whichever is less; 10 percent of 300 is 30.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(g)(4)(ii), Leak inspections
notes.evidence: the system must automatically alert the owner or operator when measurements indicate a loss of 50 pounds of refrigerant or 10 percent of the full charge, whichever is less.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: By when must the report on a chronically leaking appliance be submitted?
notes.back: By 1 March of the following year.
notes.explanation: The report must describe efforts to identify leaks and repair the appliance.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(j), Chronically leaking appliances
notes.evidence: must submit a report to EPA at the address in paragraph (m) of this section. This report must be submitted by March 1 of the subsequent year and describe efforts to identify leaks and repair the appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An R-22 appliance with a 400-pound full charge leaked 520 pounds during 2025. Is it a chronically leaking appliance, and what follows?
notes.back: Yes: 520 pounds is 130 percent of full charge, so a report is due by 1 March 2026.
notes.explanation: The threshold is 125 percent of the full charge in a calendar year, which is 500 pounds here.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(j), Chronically leaking appliances
notes.evidence: Owners or operators of appliances containing 50 pounds or more of refrigerant that leak 125 percent or more of the full charge in a calendar year must submit a report to EPA at the address in paragraph (m) of this section. This report must be submitted by March 1 of the subsequent year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An appliance with a 400-pound full charge leaked 450 pounds in one calendar year. Must it be reported as chronically leaking?
notes.back: No: 450 pounds is 112.5 percent, below the 125 percent threshold.
notes.explanation: For a 400-pound full charge the reporting line is 500 pounds in the calendar year.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.157(j), Chronically leaking appliances
notes.evidence: Owners or operators of appliances containing 50 pounds or more of refrigerant that leak 125 percent or more of the full charge in a calendar year must submit a report
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: For low-pressure appliances, what does the Type III outline say must be recovered besides liquid?
notes.back: Vapour.
notes.explanation: The item follows directly after the advice to recover liquid first to speed the process.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Recovering liquid at beginning of recovery process speeds up process - Need to recover vapor in addition to liquid

notes.front: A technician has removed the liquid from a low-pressure centrifugal chiller. Is recovery finished, according to the Type III outline?
notes.back: A) No: the vapour must be recovered too.
notes.choices:
A) No: the vapour must be recovered too
B) Yes: once the liquid is out, recovery is complete
C) Yes, if the oil has been drained
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the outline says vapour must be recovered in addition to liquid.
notes.explanation: Recovering the liquid first speeds the job, but it is not the whole job.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to recover vapor in addition to liquid

notes.front: To what temperature does the Type III outline say oil should be heated before it is removed?
notes.explanation: The outline gives the purpose as minimising refrigerant release.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to heat oil to 130°F before removing it to minimize refrigerant release

notes.front: Before draining oil from a low-pressure chiller, what does the Type III outline say to do to limit refrigerant release?
notes.back: A) Heat the oil to 130 °F.
notes.choices:
A) Heat the oil to 130 °F
B) Chill the oil first
C) Drain it cold straight away
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the outline says to heat the oil to 130 °F before removal, not to chill it or drain it cold.
notes.explanation: Heating to 130 °F is the outline's step for minimising refrigerant release when removing oil.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to heat oil to 130°F before removing it to minimize refrigerant release

notes.front: During refrigerant evacuation of a chiller, what does the Type III outline say to do with the water?
notes.back: Circulate it or remove it, to prevent freezing.
notes.explanation: Either option serves the outline's stated aim of preventing freezing.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to circulate or remove water from chiller during refrigerant evacuation to prevent freezing

notes.front: A technician will evacuate refrigerant from a centrifugal chiller while its water pumps are off and the tubes are full. What does the Type III outline say?
notes.back: A) Circulate or remove the water first, to prevent freezing.
notes.choices:
A) Circulate or remove the water first, to prevent freezing
B) Leave the water standing
C) Add nitrogen to the water side
notes.choicesExplained: B: standing water is what the outline's rule is there to avoid. C: the outline says nothing about nitrogen on the water side.
notes.explanation: The outline requires the water to be circulated or removed during evacuation.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to circulate or remove water from chiller during refrigerant evacuation to prevent freezing

notes.front: When recharging a low-pressure system, what does the Type III outline say to introduce first, vapour or liquid?
notes.back: Vapour, before liquid.
notes.explanation: The outline gives the reason: to prevent the water in the tubes from freezing.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recharging Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to introduce vapor before liquid to prevent freezing of water in the tubes

notes.front: A technician is recharging an evacuated centrifugal chiller. Which approach matches the Type III outline?
notes.back: B) Vapour first, then liquid, through the evaporator charging valve.
notes.choices:
A) Liquid first, through any convenient port
B) Vapour first, then liquid, through the evaporator charging valve
C) Liquid and vapour together, through the condenser
notes.choicesExplained: A: liquid first risks the freezing the outline warns of, and the outline names the evaporator charging valve. C: the outline gives an order, vapour before liquid, and a valve, the evaporator charging valve.
notes.explanation: Both recharging items in the outline apply at once here.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recharging Techniques”
notes.evidence: Need to introduce vapor before liquid to prevent freezing of water in the tubes - Need to charge centrifugals through evaporator charging valve

notes.front: To what level must a low-pressure appliance be evacuated before opening or disposal?
notes.back: 25 mm Hg absolute, with recovery equipment of any date.
notes.explanation: The table gives the same figure in both columns, so equipment age does not change it.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a), Table 1, Required levels of evacuation for appliances
notes.evidence: Low-pressure appliance | 25 mm Hg absolute | 25 mm Hg absolute.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An R-123 chiller (a low-pressure appliance) is being scrapped, using a recovery machine made in 1992. What evacuation level applies?
notes.back: A) 25 mm Hg absolute.
notes.choices:
A) 25 mm Hg absolute
B) 4 inches of mercury vacuum
C) 0 psig
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the older-equipment figure for medium- and some high-pressure appliances. C: 0 psig is for the non-major and leaking-component exceptions.
notes.explanation: Low-pressure appliances take 25 mm Hg absolute with old or new equipment, and disposal is covered.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a), Table 1, Required levels of evacuation for appliances
notes.evidence: Low-pressure appliance | 25 mm Hg absolute | 25 mm Hg absolute.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How does the unit of the low-pressure evacuation level differ from the other rows of Table 1?
notes.back: It is in mm Hg absolute; the other rows are in inches of mercury vacuum.
notes.explanation: The table heading gives inches of vacuum relative to 29.9 inches Hg, but the low-pressure row states its own unit.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a), Table 1, Required levels of evacuation for appliances
notes.evidence: Inches of Hg vacuum(relative to standard atmospheric pressure of 29.9 inches Hg)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: For a non-major repair not followed by evacuation to the atmosphere, what must be done to a low-pressure appliance before it is opened?
notes.back: Pressurise it to no higher than 0 psig.
notes.explanation: Openings must also be covered where isolation is not possible.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii), Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances
notes.evidence: Be pressurized to a pressure no higher than 0 psig before it is opened if it is a low-pressure appliance. Persons must cover openings when isolation is not possible.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A small non-major repair is planned on a low-pressure chiller, with no evacuation to the atmosphere afterwards. What pressure must it be at before opening?
notes.back: C) Pressurised to no higher than 0 psig.
notes.choices:
A) Evacuated to 10 inches of mercury vacuum
B) Evacuated to 25 mm Hg absolute
C) Pressurised to no higher than 0 psig
notes.choicesExplained: B: 25 mm Hg absolute is the Table 1 level, which the non-major exception replaces. A: that is a Table 1 level for other appliance types.
notes.explanation: The non-major exception applies, and for low-pressure appliances it means pressurising, not evacuating, to 0 psig.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii), Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances
notes.evidence: Be pressurized to a pressure no higher than 0 psig before it is opened if it is a low-pressure appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: For a non-major repair, how does reaching 0 psig differ between high-pressure and low-pressure appliances?
notes.back: High-pressure appliances are evacuated down to 0 psig; low-pressure appliances are pressurised up to 0 psig.
notes.explanation: The target is the same, but the direction is opposite.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Service Practice Requirements, “Repairs that are Not Major and Are Not Followed by Evacuation”
notes.evidence: For high- or very high-pressure appliances, the equipment must be evacuated to 0 psig before it is opened. - For low-pressure appliances, the equipment must be pressurized to 0 psig before it is opened.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which water-based method does the Type III outline allow for pressurising a low-pressure system for a non-major repair?
notes.back: Controlled hot water.
notes.explanation: The outline lists it as one of the allowable pressurising methods.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Requirements”
notes.evidence: Allowable methods for pressurizing a low-pressure system for a non-major repair (controlled hot water and system heating/pressurization device such as Prevac)

notes.front: Which device-based method does the Type III outline allow for pressurising a low-pressure system for a non-major repair?
notes.back: A system heating/pressurisation device such as Prevac.
notes.explanation: It is the second allowable method beside controlled hot water.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Requirements”
notes.evidence: Allowable methods for pressurizing a low-pressure system for a non-major repair (controlled hot water and system heating/pressurization device such as Prevac)

notes.front: A technician must bring a low-pressure system up to 0 psig for a non-major repair. Which is an allowable method in the Type III outline?
notes.back: C) Controlled hot water.
notes.choices:
A) Running the compressor under vacuum
B) Adding pure refrigerant
C) Controlled hot water
notes.choicesExplained: B: the outline lists no refrigerant addition as a pressurising method. A: the outline lists only controlled hot water and heating/pressurisation devices.
notes.explanation: Controlled hot water and a heating/pressurisation device such as Prevac are the outline's allowable methods.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Recovery Requirements”
notes.evidence: Allowable methods for pressurizing a low-pressure system for a non-major repair (controlled hot water and system heating/pressurization device such as Prevac)

notes.front: When pressurising a low-pressure appliance whose refrigerant boils at or below 85 °F at 29.9 inches of mercury, what may not be used?
notes.back: Methods such as nitrogen that require subsequent purging.
notes.explanation: The limit depends on the refrigerant's boiling point at standard atmospheric pressure.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii), Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances
notes.evidence: Persons pressurizing low-pressure appliances that use refrigerants with boiling points at or below 85 degrees Fahrenheit at 29.9 inches of mercury (standard atmospheric pressure), must not use methods such as nitrogen that require subsequent purging.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: When the refrigerant boils above 85 °F at 29.9 inches of mercury, how must a low-pressure appliance be pressurised?
notes.back: With heat as far as possible; nitrogen may then take it from that level to atmospheric pressure.
notes.explanation: Heat comes first; nitrogen may only make up the remaining gap to atmospheric pressure.
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.156(a)(1)(ii), Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances
notes.evidence: Persons pressurizing low-pressure appliances that use refrigerants with boiling points above 85 degrees Fahrenheit at 29.9 inches of mercury, must use heat to raise the internal pressure of the appliance as much as possible, but may use nitrogen to raise the internal pressure of the appliance from the level attainable through use of heat to atmospheric pressure
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: The Agency's service practice page names one refrigerant with which nitrogen may be used to pressurise a low-pressure appliance. Which?
notes.explanation: The page gives nitrogen as its example of a method needing later purging. The rule itself draws the line by boiling point: above 85 °F at 29.9 inches of mercury, nitrogen may follow heat.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Service Practice Requirements, “Repairs that are Not Major and Are Not Followed by Evacuation”
notes.evidence: Methods that require subsequent purging (e.g., nitrogen) cannot be used except with appliances containing R-113.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: For which refrigerant does the Type III outline say ASHRAE Standard 15 requires an equipment room refrigerant sensor?
notes.explanation: This is in addition to the oxygen deprivation sensor that the outline lists for all refrigerants.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Safety”
notes.evidence: Equipment room requirements under ASHRAE Standard 15 (oxygen deprivation sensor with all refrigerants) - Under ASHRAE Standard 15, need to have equipment room refrigerant sensor for R-123

notes.front: An equipment room houses an R-123 centrifugal chiller. Under ASHRAE Standard 15, as the Type III outline puts it, which sensors does the room need?
notes.back: B) An oxygen deprivation sensor and a refrigerant sensor.
notes.choices:
A) An oxygen deprivation sensor only
B) An oxygen deprivation sensor and a refrigerant sensor
C) No sensor
notes.choicesExplained: A: the outline adds a refrigerant sensor for R-123. C: the outline lists an oxygen deprivation sensor with all refrigerants.
notes.explanation: R-123 brings in the refrigerant sensor on top of the all-refrigerant oxygen deprivation sensor.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Type 3 (Low-pressure): Safety”
notes.evidence: Equipment room requirements under ASHRAE Standard 15 (oxygen deprivation sensor with all refrigerants) - Under ASHRAE Standard 15, need to have equipment room refrigerant sensor for R-123
